```{r}
#| label: setup
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

game_films_raw <- readr::read_csv("data/game_films.csv")
```

## Introduction

This project uses the "Films Based on Video Games" dataset, compiled from a Wikipedia list and published on TidyTuesday on 2026-06-09. It has 'r nrow(game_films_raw)' films and 'r ncol(game_films_raw)'columns, and each row is one film(theatrical,direct-to-video, television,short or documentary).Many budget,box office and score values are missing,so we focus mostly on theatrical releases.Our team chose it because video game adaptations are popular and often criticized,and we wanted to see whether they make money and how critics and audiences react.

We answer two questions.Question 1 asks whether films with bigger budgets earn a better return on investment (ROI),using budget_low' and 'budget_high'(the lowest and highest estimated budget)and 'worldwide_box_office'(total worldwide earnings).The currency columns 'budget_currency' and 'worldwide_box_office_currency' give the currency symbol of each amount, and we match budget to box office using 'title','director' and 'release_date'(the day the film came out).Question 2 asks whether critics and audiences agree and whether the gap changes over time,using 'rotten_tomatoes'(percent of positive critic reviews), 'metacritic'(critic score out of 100),'cinema_score'(audience letter grade from A+ to F) and 'release_date'.


## Question 1: [Title that matches the question, e.g. "Do bigger budgets earn a better return?"]

### Introduction

Do films based on video games earn a better return on investment (ROI) when they have bigger budgets, or do low and medium budget films do better? We define ROI as '(worldwide box office - budget)/budget', so an ROI of 1 means the film earned a profit equal to its whole budget, and a negative ROI means it lost money. To answer this we use 'budget_low' and 'budget_high', 'worldwide_box_office',the two currency columns,'release_date',and an OECD consumer price index(CPI) table that puts all money in today's USD.

We are interested in this because box office totals make expensive films look best by default,while ROI shows how much a film earned compared to what was risked.This matters for anyone deciding how much to spend on a new game adaptation.

### Approach

To compare films fairly, we first put all money on the same scale. The budget is the midpoint of 'budget_low' and 'budget_high',and both budget and box office are adjusted for inflation with the CPI of their own currency and release year,then converted to USD.We then calculate ROI, because it measures what a film earned compared to what was risked instead of rewarding big budgets by default.

We split the films into three budget groups(low, medium and high) using thirds of the budget, so each group has about the same number of films and we do not have to choose arbitrary dollar cutoffs. We chose a 'boxplot' of ROI by group,with the boxes colored by group, because it shows the median and the spread of each group,and a few huge hits do not distort it the way they would distort an average.Each film is also drawn as a dot,so the sample size stays visible.

### Analysis

```{r}
#| label: q1-data

# Step 1: Load the inflation (CPI) table and keep only the index values
CPI_raw <- readr::read_csv('00_raw_data/OECD_Table.csv')
CPI <- CPI_raw |>
  filter(UNIT_MEASURE == "IX") |>
  select(REF_AREA,TIME_PERIOD,OBS_VALUE,OBS_VALUE_TODAY)

# Step 2: Lookup table: currency symbol -> country code and exchange rate to USD
currency_country <- tibble(
  budget_currency = c("$", "¥", "£"),
  worldwide_box_office_currency = c("$", "¥", "£"),
  country_code = c("USA", "JPN", "GBR"),
  exchange_rate = c(1,0.0063,1.32))

# Step 3: Budget in today's value in USD (midpoint of low and high, adjusted with the CPI)
game_films_budget <- game_films_raw |>
  filter(!is.na(budget_currency)) |>
  mutate(
    budget_estimate = (budget_low+budget_high)/2,
    release_year = as.double(format(release_date,"%Y")))

game_films_budget <- left_join(
  game_films_budget,
  currency_country,
  by="budget_currency")

game_films_budget <- left_join(
  game_films_budget,
  CPI,
  by=c(
    "country_code"="REF_AREA",
    "release_year"="TIME_PERIOD"
    ))

game_films_budget <- game_films_budget |>
  mutate(
    budget_estimate_today = budget_estimate*(OBS_VALUE_TODAY/OBS_VALUE),
    budget_estimate_today_usd = budget_estimate_today*exchange_rate)

# Step 4: Box office in today's value in USD (same steps as the budget)
game_films_box_office <- game_films_raw |>
  filter(!is.na(worldwide_box_office_currency)) |>
  mutate(release_year = as.double(format(release_date,"%Y")))

game_films_box_office <- left_join(
  game_films_box_office,
  currency_country,
  by="worldwide_box_office_currency")

game_films_box_office <- left_join(
  game_films_box_office,
  CPI,
  by=c(
    "country_code"="REF_AREA",
    "release_year"="TIME_PERIOD"
  ))

game_films_box_office <- game_films_box_office |>
  mutate(
    worldwide_box_office_today = worldwide_box_office*(OBS_VALUE_TODAY/OBS_VALUE),
    worldwide_box_office_today_usd = worldwide_box_office_today*exchange_rate)

# Step 5: Join budget and box office (only films that have both), then compute ROI
game_films <- inner_join(
  game_films_budget,
  game_films_box_office,
  by=c("title","director","release_date"))

game_films <- game_films |>
  select(category.x:release_date,original_game_publisher.x,budget_estimate_today_usd,worldwide_box_office_today_usd) |>
  mutate(ROI = (worldwide_box_office_today_usd-budget_estimate_today_usd)/budget_estimate_today_usd) 

# Step 6: Split budget into three groups with about the same number of films
budget_cutoff <- quantile(
  game_films$budget_estimate_today_usd,
  probs = c(0,1/3,2/3,1))

game_films$budget_group <- cut(game_films$budget_estimate_today_usd,breaks=budget_cutoff,labels=c("Low\n$3-46M","Medium\n$46-92M","High\n$92-259M"),include.lowest=TRUE)
```


```{r}
#| label: q1-boxplot
#| fig-cap: "ROI by budget group"
game_films %>%
  ggplot(aes(x=budget_group, y=ROI, fill=budget_group,label=title)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.6) +
  #geom_text(aes(label=ifelse(ROI>10,as.character(title),'')),hjust=0,vjust=-0.5) +
  geom_jitter(color="black", size=0.4, alpha=0.9) + scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x, "x")) +
  scale_y_continuous(n.breaks = 20) +
  theme_minimal()+
  theme(
    legend.position="none",
    plot.title = element_text(size=11)
  ) +
  ggtitle("ROI by Budget Group") +
  xlab("")
```



### Discussion

The median ROI rises with budget: 0.68 for low (21 films),1.40 for medium (20) and 1.85 for high (20),so bigger-budget films did not earn worse returns, which is the opposite of what we expected.The low group is the least predictable.43% of its films lost money,yet it also has the biggest hit,with an ROI of 33.5,because a cheap film needs only a small box office for a large ROI.The boxes overlap a lot, so the differences between groups are small.

The boxplot shows the median, the spread and every film at once,but a few extreme hits stretch the y-axis and make the boxes hard to compare,and it does not say which films the outliers are.The results cover only 61 theatrical films,we did not look at genre,budgets do not include marketing,and box office is not profit.




## Question 2: [Title that matches the question, e.g. "Do critics and audiences agree?"]

### Introduction

[Question, variables (rotten_tomatoes, metacritic, cinema_score, release_date), why you are interested.]

### Approach

[Two different plot types and why each one is the best choice. At least one uses color or facets.]

### Analysis

```{r}
#| label: q2-data
grades <- c("A+" = 100, "A" = 97, "A-" = 93, "B+" = 90, "B" = 87, "B-" = 84,
            "C+" = 80, "C" = 77, "C-" = 74, "D+" = 70, "D" = 67, "D-" = 64, "F" = 57)

q2 <- game_films_raw |>
  mutate(audience = unname(grades[cinema_score]),
         critic   = (rotten_tomatoes + metacritic) / 2,
         gap      = audience - critic) |>
  filter(!is.na(gap))
```

```{r}
#| label: q2-gap-over-time
#| fig-cap: "Audience minus critic score over time"
ggplot(q2, aes(release_date, gap)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(color = "#08519c", size = 2.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Release date", y = "Audience minus critics (points)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
#| label: q2-biggest-gaps
#| fig-cap: "Films where audiences and critics disagreed most"
q2 |>
  slice_max(abs(gap), n = 8) |>
  ggplot(aes(reorder(title, gap), gap, fill = gap > 0)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Audience minus critics (points)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

### Discussion

[What the plots show, why, and limitations (small sample, fans may inflate CinemaScore, letter grades converted to numbers).]
